Introduction

[
1
]

McGill University seeks the issuance of an interlocutory
injunction that would prevent the blocking or obstruction of its buildings and
of all paths, streets and walkways  oo its lower campus, in downtown Montreal.
It also seeks to prevent the making of excessive noise within five meters of
its buildings, as well as the intimidation, harassment  or threatening of any
of its students, employee or representative “because [such person] is
personally associated with” McGill’s policies.

[
2
]

McGill’s request follows violent incidents that
took place on its campus in relation to the current crisis in Gaza, beginning
in February 2024 with a blockade of the Bronfman building. McGill explains that
these events would have been organized or promoted through various posts on the
Instagram page of a group that calls itself “Students For Palestine’s Honour
and Resistance” (
SPHR
), a group without legal existence that McGill has
designated as the defendant to the present proceedings.

[
3
]

McGill’s request is supported by a group of
Jewish student associations, but a number of parties have sought to intervene
to oppose the issuance of the injunction, including other Jewish student
associations and several labour unions representing McGill employees. These
interveners are concerned that the injunction requested by McGill would have a
significant chilling effect on their ability to organize their activities,
including in the context of upcoming collective agreement negotiations. They
point out that by being directed at “any person having knowledge of or having
received service of the judgment,” the Court’s orders would apply
indiscriminately to anyone on campus and beyond, whether or not that have
anything to do with SPHR, irrespective of their motiv­ations.

[
4
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court concludes
that the order requested by McGill ought not be issued. While the Court deeply
sympathizes with the concerns expressed by many members of the McGill
community, an interlocutory injunction is an exceptional form of relief that may
severely restrain individual liberty and lead to draconian conse­quences. It
should only be granted sparingly, subject to strict conditions. An injunction cannot
rest on hypothetical considerations: it is meant to respond to actual or
imminent infringements of rights that are expected to cause serious or irreparable
harm and that may only be prevented through the Court’s intervention. These
conditions are not met here.

[
5
]

The record before the Court contains no evidence
that the events McGill seeks to prohibit are likely to take place. There is no
evidence regarding who would be behind SPHR, no evidence regarding their
intentions. McGill has not either demonstrated how the injunction it seeks would
be necessary or helpful in combatting the current unhealthy atmosphere on
campus and in restoring a peaceful and respectful learning environment.

[
6
]

This is not to deny the gravity of the illegal
and intolerable events that took place last April or in the months that
preceded. These have left deep and lasting wounds for many students,
instructors and staff members. The McGill community is entitled to an
atmosphere that is free of violence, fear or harassment, and McGill is entitled
to act when necessary to ensure it is the case. An injunction, however, is not
a remedy that can be obtain as a precaution against events the likelihood of
which has not been demons­trated. Nor is it meant to be a message broadcasted
to the whole community to signify that certain acts will not be tolerated.

Factual
and procedural context

1.

The facts at the origin of the present
proceedings

[
7
]

SPHR is an unincorporated, unregistered entity
that operates an Instagram page under the handle @sphrmcgill, where it
describes itself as a “Student organization committed to Palestine’s struggle
for liberation”
[1]
. It was previously a club affiliated with McGill’s main student
association, the Students’ Society of McGill University (
SSMU
), but its
club status was revoked in September 2024
[2]
.

[
8
]

According to McGill, SPHR has been involved in
the organization of several violent events on the McGill campus. Its overall agenda
would be to pressure McGill into cutting all ties with Israeli institutions and
corporations, including all investments in firms or funds connected to Israel. It
vows that there should be “no classes or business as usual until divestment and
academic boycott”
[3]
. SPHR’s Instagram posts confirm that it encourages civil
disobedience and that it claims victory when McGill buildings and classrooms are
blockaded and classes are cancelled.

[
9
]

In February 2024, SPHR was involved with other
groups in the organization of a blockade of the Bronfman Building, home to McGill’s
Desautels Faculty of Management. In the morning of February 22, 2024, all of
the buildings’ access doors were blocked and masked protesters lined the façade,
holding large banners. This forced classes to be cancelled or moved online. Counter-protesters
gathered across the street, and police were called.

[
10
]

According to McGill, this blockade marked the beginning of a new
chapter on campus.

[
11
]

In late March 2024, SPHR participated in organizing a series of
classroom disruptions targeting the Faculties of Education, Management, and
Engineering, faculties that maintain identifiable ties with Israeli
institutions and which SPHR describes as “complicit in the occupation of
Palestine and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.” Over a few days, protesters
blocked access to several large classrooms in the buildings of the three
faculties.

[
12
]

On April 27, 2024, tents started being erected on a portion of the
lower field of McGill’s downtown campus, with apparent support and
encouragement from SPHR, who posted extensively in favour of this “Encampment.”
In the weeks that followed, two attempts were made to obtain a court order
forcing the dismantling of the Encampment; a first request was presented by two
students, and then one was presented by McGill. Both requests were dismissed
[4]
.

[
13
]

In May 2024, graffiti were left at the homes of McGill administrators,
accusing them of having “Failed the martyrs of Palestine.” A protest was also organized
in front of the home of Professor Angela Campbell, who was then interim deputy
provost of McGill and was as such involved in negotiations with the
representatives of the Encampment.

[
14
]

On June 6, 2024, a group of students occupied McGill’s James
Administration Building, blocking doors from the inside, causing extensive
damage and chanting loudly. Staff members present in the building were understandably
alarmed and fearful for their personal safety. Police had to intervene to regain
control of the building and allow staff to finally be let out. Thirteen arrests
were made.

[
15
]

Further damage occurred on the night of July 5, 2024, when
protesters moved through the downtown campus breaking windows and doors, in
apparent response to the dismantling by police and Montreal city workers of
another pro-Palestinian encampment that had been set up at Square Victoria.

[
16
]

A few days later, McGill went ahead with the dismantling of its own
on-campus Encampment. This was carried out done peacefully.

[
17
]

On September 12, 2024, five McGill classrooms were blockaded as part
of a “National Day of Action” that had been announced and later trumpeted by
SPHR. On the same day, classrooms were also blockaded at Concordia University.

[
18
]

On September 18, 2024, SPHR announced a “Week of Rage” to run from
October 7 to 11, 2024 — dates marking the one-year anniversary of the Hamas-led
attacks of October 7, 2023, which ignited the current conflict in Gaza.

[
19
]

Anticipating what could occur on that date, McGill announced that it
would move classes online and restrict access to its downtown campus, erecting
fences and requiring people to show a McGill-issued ID card to access campus
buildings.

[
20
]

McGill also petitioned the Superior Court, on an
ex parte

basis, requesting the issuance of a provisional injunction. This injunction was
granted by Justice Babak Barin on October 8, 2024
[5]
, for a
period of 10 days.

[
21
]

Despite the injunction and the measures in place, protests took
place on campus. At one point, protesters even breached one of the barriers
erected by McGill.

[
22
]

On October 18, 2024, McGill sought to renew the provisional injunction,
but its request was dismissed on October 21, 2024 by Justice Gary D.D. Morrison
[6]
. Justice Morrison found that McGill had not demonstrated the
urgency required for the renewal of the provisional injunction. He underlined
that the “Week of Rage” had passed, and that McGill had not demonstrated that
it was probable that the same type of events would occur in the next few days.

[
23
]

New episodes of violence eventually took place in February 2025,
when a group of vandals moved through campus, smashing windows and disrupting
classes.

[
24
]

On March 27, 2025, the SSMU voted in favour of a three-day strike “in
Support of Palestinian Liberation,” to be held from April 2 to 4, 2025. Although
the strike had been framed as “voluntary,” SPHR published a post encouraging
students to report professors who did not opt to cancel classes during the
strike. This raised concerns that such classes would be targeted for protests
or blockades. To prepare for the strike, McGill hired 200 additional security
agents and placed many buildings under heightened security.

[
25
]

Despite these precautions, the strike gave rise to several troubling
incidents, some involving violence. Protesters smashed windows, threw paint on
buildings, entered classrooms to urge students to walk out. Protesters also blocked
entrances to certain classrooms and interfered by making noises loud enough
that classes had to be cancelled. In certain cases, McGill security agents were
called to intervene to allow students and instructors to access or exit
classrooms, leading to some scuffles with protesters. At one point, a fire
extinguisher filled with or covered in red paint was thrown through a glass-pane
door, shattering it and splattering paint across the area, including onto a
McGill staff member.

[
26
]

McGill reports that 30 classes were cancelled during the strike.

[
27
]

In the days following the strike, McGill initiated the present
proceedings before the Superior Court, seeking provisional, interlocutory and
permanent injunction against SPHR. SSMU was initially impleaded as a
mis-en-cause.

[
28
]

McGill’s request for a provisional injunction was heard on April 10,
2025 by Justice David R. Collier. The application was opposed by the SSMU and a
group of four McGill employee unions, who indicated their intention to formally
intervene in the proceedings
[7]
.

[
29
]

On April 15, 2025, Justice Collier granted the requested 10-day provisional
injunction
[8]
.

[
30
]

On April 25, 2025, McGill sought the extension of this order through
the issuance of a safeguard order to remain in force until September 19, 2025.
Justice Daniel Urbas dismissed the request, holding that while McGill had satisfied
three of the criteria for a safeguard order (appearance of right, irreparable
harm, and balance of convenience), it had not demonstrated urgency: the strike
had ended, a level of calm had returned to campus, and no imminent threat had
been shown
[9]
.

[
31
]

McGill sought to appeal this judgment, but leave was denied on June 20,
2025
[10]
.

2.

McGill’s request for an interlocutory injunction

[
32
]

Five months after the end of the student strike
and the issuance of Justice Collier’s provisional injunction, McGill now seeks
the issuance of an interlocutory injunction which would remain in place until
the proceedings can be heard on the merits. This hearing has not been set, and
it is for now impossible to determine when the parties may be ready for same.

[
33
]

The injunctive orders that McGill seeks are essentially as follows:

[
34
]

Although these conclusions are largely the same as those contained
in Justice Collier’s judgment, it bears pointing out that McGill has somewhat
reduced the breadth of the orders it seeks.

3.

Position of the other parties

[
35
]

As stated above, SPHR is not a legal entity, and there is no
evidence in the record as to how it might be constituted, whether it has any
member or who would act or speak in its name. It was not represented at the
hearing and did not file any evidence.

[
36
]

Although SSMU had initially been impleaded by McGill,
[11]
it is no longer a party to the proceedings. McGill filed a partial
discontinuance of suit against SSMU following an agreement reached in the context
of the mediation process triggered by McGill’s April 2025 notice of intent
to terminate the memorandum of agreement in place between them.

[
37
]

McGill’s request is supported by a group of Jewish student
associations active on McGill campus: Hillel Montreal, Hillel McGill, the McGill
Jewish Law Students Association, Chabad at McGill, Israel on Campus McGill,
Students Supporting Israel at McGill, and Alpha Epsilon Pi McGill. These groups
will hereinafter be referred to as the “
Hillel interveners
.” They were
authorized to intervene by judgment dated August 4, 2025
[12]
, and
they filed a number of affidavits in support of their position.

[
38
]

As was the case before Justices Collier and Urbas, a number of
associations representing various categories of McGill employees (professors,
instructors, academic and non-academic staff) oppose McGill’s request: the Association
of McGill Professors of the Faculty of Arts (“
AMPFA
”), the Association
of McGill University Research Employees (“
AMURE
”), the Association of McGill
University Support Employees (“
AMUSE
”) and the Association of Graduate
Students Employed at McGill (“
AGSEM
”). AMPFA, AMURE, AMUSE and AGSEM
also filed affidavits in support of their position.

[
39
]

Two associations of Jewish students at McGill who oppose McGill’s
request also sought leave to intervene. These are Independent Jewish Voices
McGill and McGill Chavurah (together “
IJV and Chavurah
”). Their
intervention was authorized on September 10, 2025. Given the short time left
before the hearing scheduled on the interlocutory injunction, they were not
allowed to file affidavits or other evidence
[13]
.

[
40
]

A further association of McGill employees, the McGill University
Non-Academic Certified Association/Public Service Alliance of Canada (“
MUNACA
”)
was also authorized on the same terms as IJV and Chavurah
[14]
. AMPFA, AMURE, AMUSE, AGSEM and MUNACA will collectively be
referred to as the “
union interveners
.”

4.

The hearing and the evidence filed in the Court
record

[
41
]

The hearing on the request for interlocutory injunction was held over
two days, on September 18 and 19, 2025. Two witnesses were heard: McGill’s deputy
provost, Professor Angela Campbell, and the president of AMPFA, Professor Catherine
Leclerc.

[
42
]

Voluminous written evidence was also filed in the record, composed
of:

–

Affidavits filed by McGill, by the Hillel interveners,
and by AMPFA, AMURE, AMUSE and AGSEM, together with supporting exhibits;

–

Written examinations of the affiants of the Hillel
interveners, conducted by McGill;

–

Excerpts of oral examinations conducted by McGill
of the affiants of AMPFA, AMURE and AGSEM;

–

Excerpts of the oral examinations of McGill’s
affiants, conducted by AMPFA.

Analysis

5.

Overview of the criteria for the issuance of an
interlocutory injunction

[
43
]

An interlocutory injunction is an exceptional measure grounded in
the discretionary power of the Superior Court. The party seeking its issuance
must demonstrate that it “appears to have a right to it” and that it is
“necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice” (art. 511 C.C.P.).
Although not expressly stated in article 511 C.C.P., the applicant must also
show that the balance of convenience favors the granting of the
injunction — that is, that the harm that would result if the
injunction were refused is greater than the harm that would be caused if the
injunction were granted.

[
44
]

These three criteria — appearance of right, serious
or irreparable harm, and balance of convenience — are distinct but
interrelated. The presence of each one of them is required for the injunction
to be granted, but their assessment should be conducted globally since the
strength or weakness of each one can influence the weight to be given to the
others. This was recently explained by the Court of Appeal in the context of a request
to stay the application of a statute’s provisions, the criteria for which are
the same as those applicable to an interlocutory injunction:

[97] […] [La partie requérante]
doit démontrer qu’elle satisfait à trois critères : 1) l’existence d’une apparence
de droit suffi­sante ou, en matière constitu­tionnelle, d’une question sérieuse
à juger; 2) un préjudice irréparable en cas de refus d’octroyer la demande
de sursis; et 3) la prépondérance des incon­vénients militant en faveur d’un
sursis.

[98]   Ces critères doivent être
appréciés de manière globale, les uns par rapport aux autres, tels des vases
communicants, et non de manière séparée. Plus le droit est clair, moins le juge
doit se questionner sur les inconvénients découlant de la suspension. Inversement,
“[m]oins l’apparence de droit s’avère forte, plus la nécessité de l’examen
attentif du caractère irréparable du préju­dice s’impose, comme celle,
éventuellement, du poids des inconvé­nients”.
[15]

[
45
]

It is important to note that the criteria applicable to the granting
of an interlocutory injunction differ from those applicable at the provisional
stage (or those applicable to a safeguard order) in that there is no stand-alone
requirement to demonstrate that it is “urgent” that the injunction be granted.

6.

First step of the analysis: Appearance of right

6.1

The nature of the applicable standard

[
46
]

At the first step of the analysis, the party seeking an interlocutory
injunction must demonstrate that it has an apparent or
prima facie
right
to the requested remedy. In most cases, this criterion is not very demanding:
it is generally sufficient for the party to demonstrate that its claim is
neither frivolous nor vexatious, and the court should normally abstain from conducting
a thorough examination of the facts of the case. In
Groupe CRH Canada Inc.
,
the Court of Appel expressed it this way:

[U]ne étude préliminaire du fond du
litige doit établir qu’il y a une question sérieuse à juger. Ce critère est
généralement peu exigeant. Il suffit que la demande ne soit ni frivole ni vexatoire. Par
conséquent, un long examen du bien-fondé de la demande n’est souvent ni
nécessaire ni souhaitable, sauf cir­constances exceptionnelles — comme lorsque
l’injonction interlocutoire équi­vaut pratiquement à une disposition définitive
du litige.
[16]

[
47
]

There are a few exceptions to the application of this relatively low
standard. As mentioned by the Court of Appeal, it does not apply when granting
the interlocutory injunction would in essence result in a final disposition of
the case. Nor does it apply where the plaintiff seeks a mandatory injunction,
i.e.

an injunction that would require the defendant to undertake a positive course
of action
[17]
. This is not the case here: the injunction requested by McGill is clearly
prohibitory in nature.

[
48
]

Courts also recognize that this low standard does not apply when the
injunction seeks to restrain free speech. In
Association étudiante de l’Université
McGill v. X
[18]
, a recent case involving McGill and SSMU, the Court of Appeal emphasized
that in such circumstances, it is insufficient to demonstrate the existence of
a serious question to be tried. An injunction seeking to restrain free speech
should only be issued in the most manifest of cases, where the speech sought to
be enjoined is clearly unjustifiable:

[60]    […] [L]orsque l’injonction
interlocutoire demandée, comme en l’espèce,
vise à restreindre la liberté d’expression

[…], la jurisprudence, de façon constante, a plutôt établi que ce test
traditionnel [
i.e.
la question sérieuse à juger qui ne soit ni frivole
ni vexatoire] n’est pas alors celui qui est approprié. Lorsque l’injonction
recherchée
vise à interdire la diffusion de propos ou à autrement
restreindre la liberté d’expres­sion, ce n’est que dans les cas mani­festes et
extrêmement rares qu’une injonction pourra être prononcée
, étalon qui va
bien au-delà de la simple détermination du caractère frivole ou vexatoire d’une
question sérieuse à trancher.

[61]    La Cour suprême dans
Canada
(Commission des droits de la personne) c. Canadian Liberty Net
précise en
effet cette différence de paradigme lorsque l’enjeu d’une affaire relève de la
liberté d’expression :

[…]

[48]  Tant au Canada qu’en
Angleterre,
la jurisprudence relative aux injonctions accordées à l’égard d’allégations
de déclarations diffamatoires confirme le caractère inapproprié du critère
établi dans l’arrêt
Cyanamid
. Dans les deux pays, les tribunaux ont
refusé d’appliquer ce critère en matière d’injonctions interdisant la diffusion
de déclarations diffamatoires. Bien que la diffamation ne présente pas
exactement les mêmes caractéristiques que la propagande haineuse
discriminatoire, elle s’y apparente beaucoup plus que la restriction d’une
activité commerciale, même lorsque l’un des éléments de cette activité est un
discours. […]

[62]    Ainsi, tant la Cour suprême
que la Cour [d’appel] ont maintes fois réitéré qu’une
injonction
interlocutoire visant à interdire ou à restreindre des propos écrits ou oraux
ne doit être accordée que dans les cas les plus manifestes et extrêmement rares
,
lorsque ceux-ci sont si manifestement diffamatoires et impossibles à justifier,
qu’une poursuite en diffamation serait presque certai­nement accueillie.
[19]

[Emphasis added.
Footnotes and

underline in the original omitted]

[
49
]

According to the parties who oppose the granting of the injunction
(the union interveners, IJV and Chavurah), this increased standard would apply
in the present case. They assert that the injunction would have a substantial
chilling effect on free speech on campus, and that it could affect picketing or
other forms of mobilization on the part of unions and their members. The unions
point out that although none of them is currently on strike, two bargaining
units will be negotiating the renewal of their collective agreements in the
coming months. It is thus entirely possible that some form of labour action,
including picketing, could take place in the near future.

[
50
]

The unions explain that by their very nature, picketing and other
mobilization activities involve the assembly of large groups of people, with
the aim of attracting attention and affecting the normal operations of the
employer, including by making significant noise or, sometimes, inconveniencing people
by forcing them to navigate their way around or through throngs of assembled members.
Such action incudes a form of expression. As the Supreme Court explains in
R.W.D.S.U.

v. Pepsi-Cola Canada
:

The act of picketing involves an
element of physical presence, which in turn incorporates an expressive component.
Its purposes are usually twofold: first, to convey information about a labour
dispute in order to gain support for its cause from other workers, clients of
the struck employer, or the general public, and second, to put social and
economic pressure on the employer and, often by extension, on its suppliers and
clients
[20]
.

[
51
]

Interveners’ argument is far from frivolous, but the Court does not
agree that the present case calls for the application of a heightened standard
at the first step of the analysis.

[
52
]

Should the injunction be granted, it could certainly impact how the unions
will choose to organize their labour action. They may need to act with extra carefulness
in deciding where and how to set up picketing in order to avoid claims that
they are violating the injunction by blocking access or exit to buildings, or by
making such noise as to make it impossible for classes to be held.

[
53
]

By prohibiting people from “intimid­ating, harassing or threatening,”
the injunction would also, undoubtedly, indirectly impact free speech in that
it would affect the way certain persons choose to express themselves.

[
54
]

It does not result from this, however, that the injunction requested
by McGill is comparable to the ones analyzed in
Canadian Liberty Net
[21]
and
Association étudiante de l’Université McGill v. X
[22]
. McGill does not seek to enjoin any specific message from being
disseminated. It is not either seeking to restrain debate or prevent people
from expressing their views on campus. Indeed, McGill has made sure
not

to seek any order enjoining or limiting protests, the display of banners or the
chanting of slogans.

[
55
]

For the Court, it would be a stretch to claim that by seeking to
enjoin the blocking of entrances or the making of such noise as to make it
impossible to hold a class, McGill is in reality seeking to prevent certain
messages or restrict free expression in the way envisioned by these cases.

[
56
]

By seeking to prohibit “intimidating, harassing or threatening”
persons associated with its policies, McGill is admittedly treading closer to seeking
to limit oral or written communications, but this is hardly comparable to an
injunction seeking to prevent the communication of defamatory statements or
otherwise prohibiting the expression of ideas or messages
[23]
.

[
57
]

This is not to say that the orders sought by McGill do not raise
concerns with respect to the possibility that they may impact some people’s
freedom of expression, but simply that they cannot be assimilated to conclusions
seeking to prohibit defamatory statements or to directly limit speech in a way
that would justify the application of a heightened “appearance of right”
standard. To the extent that such orders could indirectly affect freedom of
expression or expressive behaviour, this should be taken into account at the
balance of convenience stage.

[
58
]

The Court therefore concludes that the applicable standard at the
first stage of the analysis is whether McGill’s has demonstrated a
prima
facie
case, one that raises a serious question to be tried that is neither
frivolous nor vexatious. As will be discussed in the next section, the Court
concludes that McGill has done so.

6.2

Application to the present case

[
59
]

McGill rightly argues that universities have an obligation, both
under law and pursuant to the individual contracts entered into with their
students, to carry out their academic activities, and that this requires them
to ensure that students can access classrooms, attend classes and engage in other
academic activities without the risk of being intimidated, threatened or
harassed. The standards of conduct which McGill expects from its students in
this regard are summarized in its
Code of Student Conduct and Disciplinary
Procedure
[24]
.

[
60
]

Indeed, Quebec courts have often intervened to ensure that students
are able to attend class and pursue their courses, issuing multiple injunctions
in order to prevent the blocking of classes of the intimidation of students
while they seek to attend classes
[25]
.

[
61
]

As a property owner, McGill also has a right to control access to
and use of its buildings and property, as well as to prevent its property from
being damaged
[26]
. It also has the right to prevent the blocking of access and egress
from its buildings
[27]
, if only to ensure the safety of their occupants.

[
62
]

Although the Court is not bound by the conclusions reached at
earlier steps of the present proceedings, or in the previous proceedings filed
by McGill against SPHR, it is worth mentioning that McGill’s apparent right to injunctive
remedies based on the above principles has in the course of the last year been recognized
on four occasions by judges of this Court
[28]
.

[
63
]

The Court therefore concludes that McGill has demonstrated on a
prima
facie
basis that it has an apparent right to the injunctive relief that
it seeks.

7.

Second step of the analysis: Serious or
irreparable harm

[
64
]

The second criteria McGill needs to demonstrate is that the
injunction is “necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice” (art. 511
C.C.P.). Whether this criterion is met in the present circumstances is a more
delicate issue than it may appear at first glance.

[
65
]

In the context of requests for injunctions, the question at the
heart of the analysis of the “serious or irreparable harm” criterion is often
the
nature
or
extent
of the harm complained of. In other words, courts
are often asked to determine if the harm that would be created in the absence
of the injunction is truly one that can be considered “irreparable” or at least
“serious”.

[
66
]

This is not what is at stake here: there is no doubt that the events
recounted in McGill’s proceedings have caused McGill — and the whole McGill
community — serious and, in some cases, irreparable harm. This includes property
damage, stress and anxiety suffered by students, instructors and staff members,
as well as time and energy lost as a result of classes being cancelled. Should
similar events occur again, it is clear that they would likely cause the same
kind of serious or irreparable harm.

[
67
]

What is really at stake in the present proceedings is not so much
the nature or extent of the prejudice McGill seeks to avoid, but rather whether
granting the injunction is “necessary to prevent” such prejudice from occurring,
as provided by article 511 C.C.P.

[
68
]

In requiring that the injunction be “necessary to prevent” the harm
from occurring, article 511 C.C.P. does not simply require that the Court
evaluate the type of prejudice the plaintiff complains of. It requires that the
Court determine whether the prejudice would in fact occur should the injunction
not be granted — or how likely it is that the prejudice would occur —, and that
it evaluates to what extent the injunction would prevent such a prejudice from
occurring.

[
69
]

As appears from the reasons that follow, the Court concludes that
McGill has not made such a demonstration here: there is no indication that the
harm complained of by McGill is likely to occur if the injunction is not
issued, and no evidence that the injunction would alleviate what McGill and the
Hillel interveners present as a deleterious or harmful atmosphere on campus.

7.1

McGill has not demonstrated that serious or
irreparable harm is likely to occur if the injunction is not granted

[
70
]

Although McGill does not agree with this qualification, what it seeks
is essentially a “
quia timet
” or “precautionary” injunction. McGill seeks
to be better prepared to respond should it see past events occur again.

[
71
]

In his oft-quoted treatise on the law of injunction, Justice Robert
J. Sharpe writes that “[a]ll injunctions are future
looking in the sense that they are intended to prevent or avoid harm rather
than compensate for an injury already suffered in his
often-quoted treatise”
[29]
. This
being said, there is a distinction between cases where the conduct complained
of is already underway (whether or not the alleged harm is already being
suffered or is expected to begin at a later point
[30]
) and
cases where what is sought to be enjoined is future conduct that has not yet
occurred, or where the alleged harm is uncertain to follow from the conduct
complained of.

[
72
]

Where the impugned conduct is already underway and the prejudice it
causes or will cause is known, “the situation has crystallized in the sense
that the defendant’s course of conduct is settled, its effect upon the
plaintiff is known and the relative benefits to the plaintiff, and the burdens
an injunction would impose on the defendant, can be assessed”
[31]
.

[
73
]

On the contrary, when the harm has yet to occur and would only result
in the event that the defendant engages in a conduct that is as yet uncertain,
the Court is faced with having to predict what could
potentially
happen:

Where the harm to the plaintiff has
yet to occur the problems of prediction are encountered. Here, the
plaintiff sues
quia timet
– because he or she fears – and the
judgement as to the propriety of injunctive relief must be made without the
advantage of actual evidence as to the nature of harm inflicted on the
plaintiff. The court is asked to predict that harm will occur in the future and
that the harm is of a type that ought to be prevented by injunction. Thus,
while all injunctions involve predicting the future, the label
quia
timet
and the problem of prematurity relate to the situation where the
difficulties of prediction are more acute in that the plaintiff is asking for
injunctive relief before any of the harm to be prevented by the injunction has
been suffered.
[32]

[
74
]

Courts have the power to issue
quia timet
or precautionary
injunctions. When requested to do so, however, they should adopt “a cautious
approach” and require “that there […] be a high degree of probability that the
harm will in fact occur”
[33]
.

[
75
]

The Court of Appeal confirmed the need for such
caution in
Association générale des étudiants de la Faculté des lettres et
sciences humaines de l’Université de Sherbrooke v. Roy Grenier
[34]
. That case confirms that even when
considering an injunction seeking to enjoin conduct that has already taken
place in the past, a court should not issue an interlocutory injunction unless
the evidence demonstrates a high likelihood that the prejudice will occur
again.

[
76
]

The facts of that case bear some similarity to the present one: further
to a student strike that had seen its share of violence and aggressivity
between pro- and anti-strike factions, a group of students sought an injunction
to prohibit the student association (and any persons having knowledge of the
injunction) from blocking access to classes, disrupting courses or threatening,
intimidating or insulting students attending classes. The Superior Court issued
a provisional injunction (which had not been entirely respected by everyone)
and was now being called to extend its application by issuing an interlocutory  injunction.
On the day prior to the hearing on the interlocutory injunction, however, the
student association voted against an immediate continuation of the strike.

[
77
]

The student association argued that the interlocutory injunction
should not be issued because there was no immediate threat that the strike
would resume. For their part, the plaintiffs insisted that the risk was still
present since a new general assembly had been convened and would take place
prior to the hearing on the merits.

[
78
]

The Superior Court agreed with plaintiffs and issued the
interlocutory injunction, reasoning that the defendant could not avoid the
issuance of an interlocutory injunction by deciding not to continue the strike
for the time being while at the same time leaving open the possibility that it
could resume at a later date
[35]
.

[
79
]

The student association appealed.

[
80
]

Writing for the Court, Justice Marie-France Bich emphasizes the
extraordinary nature of injunctions and the fact that specific evidence is
required to demonstrate that their issuance is necessary to prevent harm:

[39]   L’injonction interlocutoire,
remède discrétionnaire, impose la contrainte judiciaire à une partie, à la
demande d’une autre, alors que leurs droits respectifs n’ont pas été examinés
de manière définitive, sur la base d’une preuve complète. Son caractère
provisionnel et ses conséquences draconien­nes en font une mesure
exceptionnelle, qui ne saurait être accordée qu’avec parcimonie, dans le
respect de conditions strictes.
Elle ne se satisfait pas de considérations
hypothétiques et ne peut être prononcée en l’absence d’une atteinte actuelle ou
imminente à un droit apparent, atteinte dont la survenance causerait un
préjudice irréparable qu’on cherche donc à limiter ou prévenir
.
[36]

[Emphasis added]

[
81
]

Justice Bich then explains that despite the high degree of deference
that is normally due to discretionary orders, the Court of Appeal is justified
in intervening to quash the injunction. Because the evidence did not show a
sufficient likelihood that irreparable harm would occur, the injunction should
not have been granted:

[41] […] [L]a déférence est de mise
à l’endroit de la décision du juge saisi d’une demande d’injonction
interlocutoire, qui jouit à cet égard d’un pouvoir d’appré­ciation dont l’exercice
doit ordinairement être respecté par la Cour.

[42] Malgré cette déférence,
toutefois, les circonstances sont telles qu’une intervention est requise. Au
moment du prononcé du jugement de première instance, en effet,
l’atteinte au
droit qu’allèguent les intimés au soutien de leurs prétentions avait cessé et
aucun préjudice irréparable n’était à craindre, sinon de manière hypothétique
ou théorique
. Cela aurait dû mener au rejet de la demande, comme le veut
une règle jurisprudentielle qui n’est pas nouvelle.
Il n’y avait pas ici,
selon la preuve même dont disposait le juge, de “forte probabilité” ou de
“probabilité sérieuse” que l’atteinte se perpétue, du moins à court ou moyen
terme
, et qu’en découle un préjudice irréparable, les tribu­naux devant
généralement se retenir d’agir “lorsque l’éventualité d’un dommage futur n’est
guère probable”.
[37]

[Emphasis added]

[
82
]

The situation here is not exactly the same. There is no evidence that
SPHR would have decided to suspend its calls to action for the time being. Yet,
there is surprisingly little in the record to support McGill’s contention that serious
prejudice will occur or is likely to occur if the injunction is not granted.

[
83
]

In addition to pointing to past events and arguing that they could
well occur again, all that McGill points to are Instagram posts by which SPHR
vows not to cease its action until its demands of divestment have been met:

“w
e
reiterate; there will be no classes or business as usual until divestment and
academic boycott” (
Exhibit
P-13)

“Until McGill cuts all financial
and academic ties with the Zionist regime, students will carry out a forceful
campaign of escalation”
(
Exhibit
P-19)

“There will be no business or class
as usual long [
sic
] as our administration remains complicit in the Zionist
genocide in Gaza”
(
Exhibit
P-25)

“
no
business or classes as usual during the university funded genocide in Gaza” (
Exhibit
P-26)

[
84
]

These posts are of course concerning. At the same time, it must be
recognized that these messages were all posted more than one year ago. They
were respectively published on March 29, 2024 (Exhibit P-13)
[38]
, June 6, 2024 (Exhibit P‑19), September 17, 2024 (Exhibit
P-25) and September 18, 2024 (Exhibit P-26).

[
85
]

In fact, McGill acknowledges that SPHR has published no post at all
since April 2025, when SPHR encouraged students to report the instructors who
were not “complying” with the strike. McGill also filed in evidence copies of posts
that would have been published in April 2025 on
other
Instagram accounts
[39]
, but there is no evidence regarding who would be behind these
accounts.

[
86
]

McGill suggests that such silence likely means that SPHR has somehow
decided to “keep quiet” in light of the injunction issued by Justice Collier on
April 15, 2025, or in light of the risk of further judicial orders. There is however
simply no evidence to support such a claim.

[
87
]

At the hearing, Professor Campbell indicated that she would have somehow
heard that “something” would be planned to mark the second anniversary of the October
7, 2023 attacks, and that there would be mobilisation in view of a student
strike on that day. She did not specify what was said, when or by whom, and it
is therefore impossible to attribute any probative value to what she would have
heard. McGill has filed no other evidence in this regard.

[
88
]

This total lack of evidence regarding the risk of future harm is
perplexing, but it is not the Court’s role to fill in the gaps left by a party’s
choice not to adduce evidence.

[
89
]

To paraphrase the Court of Appeal in
Roy Grenier
[40]
, there is simply no evidence of a “high likelihood” or “serious
likelihood” (“
forte probabilité
” or “
probabilité sérieuse
”) that the
events complained of will occur again, at least in the short or medium term.

[
90
]

Before moving on to another aspect of McGill’s claim regarding
serious or irreparable harm, it must be emphasized that the above analysis
should not be read as requiring the demonstration of some sort of “urgency” at
the interlocutory injunction stage. While urgency is usually an important criterion
for the granting of a provisional injunction or safeguard order, a party
seeking an injunction at the interlocutory stage does not need to demonstrate
urgency.

[
91
]

This is not to say, however, that an injunction should be granted even
if the alleged prejudice is not likely to occur. To issue an injunction when it
is not likely to serve any purpose would be contrary to the principle that an
injunciton is and should remain an exceptional remedy, to be issued only when strictly
necessary to prevent an “actual or imminent” infringement of a
prima facie

right that would cause serious or irreparable harm
[41]
. As Justice Gonthier writes in
I.A.T.S.E. v. Société de la Place
des Arts de Montréal
:

[An injunction] is an exceptional
and discretionary form of relief. The court will not grant an injunction
under arts. 751
et seq.
[now 509 C.C.P.] simply because
the applicant is strictly entitled to one.  The applicant must also
demonstrate
that the circumstances warrant such a potentially intrusive
remedy
, and that he is deserving of it.
[42]

7.2

McGill has not demonstrated that the injunction would
help alleviate the current harmful climate on campus

[
92
]

To be fair with McGill, the serious or irreparable harm it alleges
is not only the risk of repetition of the violent acts that occurred during the
April 2025 strike or in the preceding months. McGill — supported in this regard
by the Hillel interveners — also claims that the current atmosphere on campus is
one of unease and apprehension, that it is anxiety-inducing for many students, and
that it causes serious or irreparable harm to many members of the McGill
community.

[
93
]

The evidence filed by McGill and the Hillel interveners is extremely
troubling. It demonstrates that multiple incidents with very real antisemitic
undertones have taken place on campus since October 2023, from vandalism to
personal insults and derogatory acts directed at Jewish students. The Court
does not take this evidence lightly. These acts, which the Hillel interveners
present as a form of harassment and intimidation, are clearly unacceptable and
must be condemned.

[
94
]

There is however no evidence that the injunction McGill seeks would
do anything to alleviate the current deleterious atmosphere or prevent derogatory
acts from taking place in the future. McGill insists that it does not seek to limit
or curb free expression in any way: it seeks no conclusions prohibiting the
broadcasting of any sort of message, it does not seek to prevent people from
protesting or expressing their criticism of Israel or its policies, or even
from expressing views that could be considered antisemitic or be motivated by
antisemitism.

[
95
]

McGill does seek to order SPHR and anyone having knowledge of the
injunction from “intimidating, harassing or threatening […] any identifiable student,
employee or representative of McGill”, but only to the extent that such
intimidation, harassment or threat is motivated by the fact that the person “is
personally associated with the McGill policies that are being protested”
[43]
. One could argue that such an order would potentially prohibit certain
extreme examples of insults or derogatory remarks directed at people of the Jewish
faith or at people who support Israel’s current policies, but the evidence is
wholly insufficient to support the argument that the injunction would have any
meaningful impact on the occurrence of such regrettable acts.

[
96
]

As such, to the extent that the serious or irreparable harm alleged
by McGill is the harmful climate that would now exist on campus, neither McGill
nor the Hillel interveners have shown that the requested injunction would serve
to prevent its continuation.

7.3

Conclusion regarding serious or irreparable harm

[
97
]

While McGill has shown that serious and irreparable harm has in the
past been caused by the events it seeks to prevent from reoccurring, there is
no evidence to support the likelihood of such events occurring again in the
short to medium term. In fact, the evidence in this regard is wholly lacking.
The evidence does not either support the proposition that issuing the requested
injunction would do anything to curb the behaviour and the remarks which the
Hillel interveners present as being antisemitic or help restore a better
climate on campus.

[
98
]

The Court thus concludes that McGill has failed to demonstrate that
the requested injunction is necessary to prevent serious or irreparable harm within
the meaning of article 511 C.C.P.

8.

Third step of the analysis: Balance of
convenience

[
99
]

The party seeking an interlocutory injunction must also demonstrate
that if the injunction is refused, it will suffer a greater prejudice than that
which would be caused to the defendant (or to others, as the case may be) if
the injunction were issued.

[
100
]

The Court of Appeal has often reiterated that the balance of
convenience must
always
be considered before issuing an interlocutory
injunction, irrespective of the strength of the apparent right. In
Groupe CRH
, Justice Marie-Josée Hogue explains that although
courts occasionally affirm that it is only when a right is “doubtful” that balance
of convenience must be considered, such an approach is ill-founded
[44]
. Similarly, in
HRM Projet Children
, Justice Robert Mainville
insists that even though the criteria for the issuance of an interlocutory
injunction are interrelated, even the existence of a clear right and the
demonstration of substantial irreparable harm do not dispense with the
obligation of taking into account the balance of convenience
[45]
.

[
101
]

Assessing on which side the balance of convenience tips is often difficult.
It is especially so in circumstances where what is at stake is not simply the
commercial or financial interests of two private parties but rather a multitude
of rights and interests of a great number of people. That is the case here. Essentially,
the Court is being asked to weigh the potential impacts — positive and negative
— of granting or refusing the injunction on McGill University, on its students,
its instructors, its staff and all the visitors to its campus. It must compare
the benefits which McGill and the Hillel interveners claim would be brought by
the injunction with the harm and inconvenience the unions, IJV and Chavurah
claim it would bring about.

8.1

The parties’ position regarding balance of
convenience

[
102
]

McGill and the Hillel interveners argue that there is no real balance
of convenience argument against granting the injunction since the behaviours it
seeks to enjoin could all be described as illegal or wrongful. They point to
the fact that blocking the doors of a building or a classroom can never be
justified, that harassing, threatening or intimidating a person is always
unacceptable, if not outright contrary to the provisions of the
Criminal
Code
. They argue that no one can claim to suffer harm from being prevented
to commit illegal or wrongful acts. Despite its superficial appeal, this argument
is not entirely convincing.

[
103
]

Firstly, it is not sufficient to claim than an injunction will not
harm the defendant because he can no right to do what the injunction seeks to
enjoin. As the Supreme Court explains in
Aetna Financial Services v.
Feigelman
, “the question is not whether the injunction will harm the
defendant, but whether it is probable that unless the defendant is restrained,
wrongful acts will be done which will do the plaintiff irreparable injury”.
[46]

[
104
]

Secondly, the Court cannot restrict its analysis to considering the legal
definition of the acts that would be expressly enjoined. The Court must look at
the overall impact that the injunction is likely to have, including the “chilling
effect” it will undoubtedly create. An injunction is an exceptional remedy in
large part because of the exceptional sanction it carries. For this reason, as
Justice Gonthier explains in
I.A.T.S.E.
, “[i]t is no exaggeration to say
that injunctive relief amounts to a judicially imposed restraint on the liberty
of the person against whom it is ordered”
[47]
. It
is accordingly imperative that an injunction be specific in its targets, both
with respect to the acts it forbids and to the individuals it applies to.

[
105
]

The union interveners argue that granting the injunction would affect
their ability to mobilize their members on campus, whether for picketing or
other forms of group gathering designed to attract attention and exert pressure
on the university. They explain that they have recently organized events that
could well have been seen as infringing on the orders sought by McGill. For
instance, when AMPFA filed its initial application for certification, in April
2024, it organized a gathering of its members on the steps of the Arts Building.
According to AMPFA’s president, Professor Leclerc, union members were pretty
much “blocking” the entrance. She explains that while not completely preventing
people from getting through, “
on bloquait pas mal l’entrée
”
[48]
. Union members were also loudly chanting their slogans and using
megaphones.

[
106
]

Would this have violated the orders McGill now seeks? McGill insists
that it would not. It explains that it has narrowed down the scope of the
requested conclusions to ensure that such events would not be caught up by the
injunction’s wording. For instance, whereas the order issued by Justice Collier
prohibited people from “blocking or otherwise obstructing,
in whole or in
part
, the entrance or exits to any buildings”, McGill has withdrawn the
phrase “in whole or in part”. For McGill, this makes it clear that what would
be prohibited is to make it physically
impossible
to access buildings,
and that it would not prevent people from congregating in such a way as to reduce
the flow of people or render access merely more challenging.

[
107
]

McGill has also narrowed down the scope of the conclusion regarding “excessive
noise”. To the conclusion prohibiting people from “making excessive noise”, it
has added the phrase “such that academic, research, or other University
activities
cannot
continue.”
[49]
For
McGill, such a standard is not subjective and open to interpretation but rather
objective.

[
108
]

These efforts on the part of McGill are laudable. They not only narrow
the scope of the behaviours that it seeks to enjoin but also contribute to
making them more specific, less open to debate and interpretation. However,
this does not entirely solve the difficulties raised by the unions: why refer
to “otherwise obstructing” if all that McGill means is that entrances or exits
should not be entirely blocked off? How does one judge whether noise is so loud
that a class “cannot continue”?

[
109
]

The unions argue that if they receive requests for legal advice from
members seeking to congregate in the way that AMPFA members did in April 2024,
they will be hard pressed to provide clear advice and will be forced to err on
the safe side by recommending that members refrain from anything that could
conceivably be seen as violating the injunction, no matter how solid an
argumentation could be made that they do not constitute a violation.

[
110
]

McGill insists that the risks of being found in contempt of court
for violating an injunction should not be overstated, especially given the
standard of proof that applies to contempt charges
[50]
. This
is not entirely reassuring. Few people would be willing to take the chance that
their conduct could be
construed
as a violation, even erroneously. Faced
with uncertainty, it can be assumed that most people will
choose to err on the side of restraint.

[
111
]

This is not to say — and this point bears emphasizing — that an
injunction must always be drafted in language that is so clear, so specific,
and so devoid of any potential for misinterpretation that it can be applied
mechanically, robotically. Not everything can be reduced to a mathematical
formula that can be applied without the need for human interpretation or
judgment. When evaluating the balance of convenience, however, the Court must
take into account the potential risks that the injunction could be misinterpreted
or misapplied, and the impact of same on the people to whom it applies.

8.2

The balance of convenience associated with the
conclusions sought by McGill

[
112
]

The conclusions sought by McGill are by no means unheard of in the
context of injunctions seeking to restrain demonstrations, and efforts have
been made by McGill to ensure that they are as narrow, as clear and as
objective as possible. In another context, such conclusions might raise little concern.
Three aspects of the present case are however susceptible of creating
uncertainty and substantially increasing the inconv­enience associated with
granting the injunction: the absence of any identifiable defendant, the area
covered by the injunction, and the temporal scope of the injunction. These will
be looked at in turn.

[
113
]

Firstly, McGill has not identified any “real” defendant and is
instead seeking an injunction that would essentially apply to anyone,
irrespective of the context of their action.

[
114
]

As stated above, SPHR is not a legal entity and
there is no evidence as to how it may have been constituted. As such, including
“SPHR” as a defendant appears to be of little practical effect. To be clear,
the Court expresses no opinion on whether an injunction can be issued against
an entity with no legal existence; it merely observes that issuing the
requested injunction against SPHR would likely serve no real purpose.

[
115
]

McGill has chosen to file no evidence regarding the individuals that
may be behind SPHR or the @sphrmcgill Instagram page, regarding its attempts to
identify those individuals, or regarding its reasons for not attempting to.
According to McGill, SPHR has been active since at least October 2023, two
years ago. Representatives of SPHR have participated in many activities on
campus during that period. When protesters barricaded themselves in the James
Administration building, in June 2024, allegedly at the behest of SPHR,
thirteen arrests were made. This suggests that had McGill attempted to identify
certain of the individuals involved in SPHR, it could have. This would have
allowed the injunction to be targeted at the individuals whose conduct gave
rise to the proceedings.

[
116
]

That an injunction applies to “any person having knowledge of or
having received service of the judgment” is not unheard of either. Such injunctions
are frequent
[51]
. Most of the time, however, such wording is used in the context of
conclusions directed at an identifiable defendant and the individuals through
which it acts (directors, officers, employees, agents, etc.). The additional
reference to “any person having knowledge of the order” is meant to ensure that
the injunction remains effective even if the person carrying out the prohibited
acts is not under the defendant’s authority or control.

[
117
]

Such a context is absent here. Nothing in the injunction’s wording would
restrict its application to persons acting under the control or at the behest
of SPHR. It would apply to anyone on campus (and beyond) who knows of the order’s
existence, irrespective of their motivation. Provided they have been informed
of the order, it would apply to McGill students, to employees exercising their
collective rights as union members (whether they are members of the interveners
or other unions), to any protesters (whether they are protesting the situation
in Gaza, the climate crisis or any other situation), or anyone else on campus that
happens to be making excessive noise.

[
118
]

The orders prohibiting intimidation, harassment or threatening of students,
employees or representatives associated with McGill policies would not be
limited to its policy concerning Israel or the situation in Gaza. It would apply
irrespective of the nature of the McGill policies being protested, whether it
be student fee hikes or anything else.

[
119
]

There is of course no indication that McGill intends to use the
injunction in such a way, but nothing in the order would prevent it from being
used in a context that has nothing to do with the circumstances that led to its
issuance.

[
120
]

As the Newfoundland and Labrador Court of
Appeal explains in a 2019 case concerning protests against the Muskrat Falls
hydro-electric project
[52]
, courts should be reluctant to grant injunctions that would enjoin
conduct unrelated to the specific actions of the defendant that are being
complained of and that justified the court in granting relief:

[28] […]
[T]he establishment of
a cause of action leading to the decision to grant an injunction is not a free
ticket to protection by injunction of every legal and proprietary right held by
the injunction-seeker. Only those rights which the claimant has asserted have
been interfered with in the lawsuit are eligible for protection by injunction

and the consequent contempt power, and then only if the court decides to
exercise its discretion to grant an injunction and only to the extent they have
been interfered with or threatened to be interfered with.
Other rights,
especially proprietary rights, that are not in issue in the lawsuit should not
be protected. The protection of those rights should be left to separate action

[…].

[29]    The court considering
granting an injunction should therefore be cautious to ensure that
the
language employed in the injunction prohibition does not extend to enjoining
activities that are not being complained about
. To do other­wise
risks
dragging persons and activities under the umbrella of injunction protection
that cannot be justified by the claims that have been advanced
.
[53]

[Emphasis added]

[
121
]

Justice Sharpe expresses a similar point of view:

It has been forcefully argued that
the willingness to enforce injunc­tions against non-parties has been taken too
far. The net of liability is not cast too wide where the plaintiff is able to
show that the non-party has deliberately agreed to flout the order at the
instigation of the defendant. However, the court must be cautious not to hold
in contempt
a party who acts indepen­dently of the defend­ant and who may
exercise a right distinct from that of the defendant. Such a person has not yet
had his or her day in court and should not be bound by an order made in an
action to which he or she was not a party
[…].
The court should not
simply delegate to the police the power to determine who is covered by the
injunction: the alleged contemnors are entitled to their day in court
.
[54]

[Emphasis added]

[
122
]

These concerns are directly applicable here. Despite McGill’s good faith
attempt to narrow the scope of the orders, they would apply to persons and
activities that have nothing to do with the claims that have been advanced by McGill
and that would here justify the granting of the injunction.

[
123
]

Secondly, the difficulty associated with the undetermined breadth of
the injunction is compounded by the area over which it would apply. What is
sought to be enjoined is not blocking one, or two, or three specific entrances,
but all “the entrances and exists to any buildings, paths, streets, or walkways”
on McGill’s Lower Campus, which comprises dozens of buildings and a great
number of paths and walkways, as well as “any buildings identified as being
used for McGill’s operations”, wherever situated.

[
124
]

As for the orders regarding intimidating, harassing or threatening
persons, it’s application would not be limited geographically. It would apply wherever
the alleged actions take place, whether on or off campus, in Montreal or
elsewhere.

[
125
]

The third aspect of McGill’s request which the Court sees as being problematic
is its temporal duration. When an injunction is issued for a limited duration,
in response to an urgent situation created by an impending or actual crisis, the
fact that it may be overbroad or insufficiently specific can be of limited consequence,
and the court may well be satisfied that granting the injunction is justified
even though it could potentially lead to unintended consequences.

[
126
]

In such instances, the inconvenience caused by the granting of the
injunction is limited by its short duration. It may thus be insufficient
overall to tip the balance of convenience against granting the injunction. Indeed,
when McGill requested the issuance of provisional injunctions in relation to
SPHR’S activities, the court each time concluded that the balance of
convenience favoured the granting of the injunction.

[
127
]

The situation is now substantially different. The injunction McGill
seeks would apply for an indeterminate period of time. The inconvenience it would
cause would thus also continue for the same indeterminate time.

[
128
]

For these reasons, the Court concludes that the balance of
convenience does not favour the granting of the injunction requested by McGill.

COnclusion

[
129
]

At the hearing, McGill and the Hillel interveners insisted that the
situation on campus was such that “
something
had to be done”. For them, the
granting of the injunction would be a message send to the whole McGill
community that their university will not tolerate acts of violence,
intimidation or disorder, whereas the Court’s refusal to grant the injunction would
be the equivalent of saying that “nothing can be done” in response to violence,
disorder and disrespect on campus. The Court disagrees with this way of
portraying the situation.

[
130
]

In legal proceedings, the party seeking the court’s intervention must
demonstrate that it meets the legal requirement for the granting of the specific
remedy it seeks. This is especially true in the context of injunction, an
extraordinary remedy to be issued only in exceptional cases. McGill chose to
seek the granting on an interlocutory injunction. It determined the nature of
the orders it was seeking and the evidence to put forward in support of its
request. It had the obligation to demonstrate to the Court that the evidence
justified the granting of the injunction it sought. This demonstration was not
made.

[
131
]

What happened on McGill’s campus in April 2025 and in the months
that preceded was illegal, unacceptable and unjustifiable. Nothing in the Court’s
refusal to grant an interlocutory injunction should be seen as condoning what
happened. While the Court deeply sympathizes with the
concerns expressed by McGill and by many students and members of its larger community,
it must conclude that the granting of the requested injunction is not warranted
by the evidence.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
132
]
